projects.title: Geometry Of Poker
projects.description: Geometry of Poker is a production-deployed research visualization for Texas Hold'em state space. It converts poker states into compact feature vectors, embeds those vectors into a three-dimensional manifold, and serves the resulting map as an interactive GPU point cloud.

I've spent some time during the summer reading "GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA" by Paulo Motta, Ph.D. What stuck with me wasn't another walkthrough of CUDA kernels. It was the engineering mindset behind the book. A few things stood out, as someone who spends a lot of time thinking about performance in modern C++: 1. GPU programming as engineering, not just kernels - Testing with Google Test and Pytest. - Profiling with Nsight Compute. - Knowing when to reach for cuBLAS or Thrust instead of writing a custom kernel. This is how real production systems get built. 2. Hardware understanding over blind offloading. Performance isn't just faster kernels. It's PCIe bandwidth, data transfer sizes, overlapping communication with computation, and knowing where the real bottleneck sits. The same questions we ask when optimizing CPU-bound low-latency systems. 3. The C++/Python bridge Exposing GPU-accelerated C++ libraries to Python, without unnecessary NumPy copies. Increasingly relevant when Python handles orchestration and C++ handles execution. 4. Written for C++ dev, not GPU researchers The examples build up gradually, stay focused on programming, and skip the math barrier that keeps a lot of C++ developers away from GPU work. My takeaway: - Whether you're optimizing a low-latency trading engine or a GPU workload, the principles don't change. - Understand the hardware. Measure before you optimize. - Treat performance as an engineering discipline, not a collection of tricks. Recommended for any C++ developer curious about GPU computing who isn't sure where to start.

Over the last month I "vibe researched" several PhDs' worth of maths results in and around the field I did my research in 25+ years ago (complete with Lean formalization and passable text). This includes a counterexample to a top-5 major conjecture in the field! I assume any active researcher in the field would have done even better. What does this mean for the bar for a "significant" maths contribution going forward? Clearly you can't just give out PhDs for what I did, so the bar must already be much higher today (even if nothing better than 5.6 shows up), not in some kind of distant and hypothetical future. And if the gap between "5.7" and 5.6 is the same size as the gap between 5.6 and 5.5, we are talking mostly superhuman performance in all aspects of maths. We are going to see 50 years' worth of maths progress in the next 2 years, but there won't be nearly enough human mathematicians around to process and understand all of it, let alone figure out how to apply it all or what new questions to ask.

At YC Startup School 2026, I posted a photo of Alexandr Wang ’s “top 10 mane.” Alexandr replied. Y Combinator reposted another post, and Garry Tan reposted another photo from the same afternoon. The throwaway jokes and ramblings reached 111.3k views. A couple months earlier, I spoke with Evil Rabbit , Vercel’s founding designer and former head of design, at Designers & Machines. I've met YC founders at my climbing gym, gotten hats and a JBL from VC partners, got sushi with a member of OpenAI. I met an OpenAI intern who once carried a briefcase with GPT-4o's parameters, and the friend of the owner of Molly Tea’s New York franchises explaining why they split from the China business. This keeps happening here. SF is so small that you keep running into the craziest people, and they can just as easily find you. The most memorable line from Startup School came from Alexandr: start from first principles. He built Scale AI after training-data friction blocked his own work. SF has a social version of that lesson. Put enough builders, designers, researchers, and founders into 49 square miles. Keep showing up. The people you follow become conversations. The conversations expose problems. Then the problems become things worth building. The talks were fantastic, but the city around them has been the real school 🌁
